name: The EU AI Act for Pharma and MedTech
blurb: How the AI Act applies to drugmakers and device makers, and when.
title: The EU AI Act for Pharma and MedTech
answer: The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 with duties phasing in. Its AI literacy duty in Article 4 applied from 2 February 2025, making it the first obligation pharma companies had to meet. AI in medical devices that need notified body review counts as high risk, while most research, manufacturing and back office AI faces lighter or voluntary rules unless used in a high risk context.

reading.body:
The EU AI Act's first duty to bind pharma and medtech was not about high-risk devices but about staff: AI literacy applied from 2 February 2025.

The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and phases its duties in. Article 4 arrived first, requiring providers and deployers to ensure the people using AI understand it. For life sciences teams this inverts the usual compliance instinct, which is to start with the riskiest system. The earliest enforceable obligation is an inventory and training problem, not a validation problem.

Risk classification then splits the sector. AI in a medical device that needs notified body review is high risk, and device makers carry AI Act conformity alongside MDR or IVDR. Most research, manufacturing and back office AI faces lighter or voluntary rules, unless it is used in a high risk context. That qualifier does the work: a model is not exempt because of where it sits, but because of what it decides.

The data covers two dated milestones and the classification principle. It does not give the later phase-in dates, the penalties, or the standards a device maker would conform against. Treat it as the shape of the obligation, not the compliance plan.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.

The requirement that a person can understand, intervene in, and override AI decisions. Mandated for high-risk uses under the EU AI Act, and only real when the human has the time, information, and authority to actually intervene.
An accredited organization designated to carry out third-party conformity assessment under EU product law.

Baseline workforce understanding of AI capability, limits, and policy: what the tools can do, where they fail, and what the rules are. Under the EU AI Act it is now a legal requirement for providers and deployers, not just good practice.
The European regulation classifying AI systems by risk, with obligations scaled to each tier: prohibited, high-risk, limited, minimal.

explainer:
The AI Act classifies AI systems by risk. A small set of practices is banned outright, high risk systems face the heaviest duties, systems that interact with people carry transparency duties, and general purpose AI models have their own obligations for their providers. For life sciences the most direct effect is on medical devices: AI that is part of a device requiring notified body assessment under the Medical Device or In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation is high risk, which brings duties on risk management, data quality, documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

For most pharma uses, research, manufacturing support, safety processing and internal productivity, the Act's heavier duties do not apply unless a system falls into a listed high risk area such as employment decisions. The duty that applies to everyone is AI literacy: since February 2025 providers and deployers must take measures so that staff using AI understand it well enough for their role. Companies should keep an inventory of AI systems, classify each, and keep evidence of training.

developments.text: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, entered into force.
The AI literacy obligation became applicable: providers and deployers must ensure staff using AI have sufficient understanding of it.
